title: Traders, not armies
hookLine: Islam reached much of Southeast Asia through merchants and teachers

lines: A SHIP WAITING FOR THE WIND.
A NEW PART: EAST AND SOUTHEAST ASIA.
cards: A ship sits in harbor on the coast of Sumatra, waiting for the wind to turn. It could be weeks. The merchants aboard can't sail home until the monsoon shifts, so they come ashore.
They rent rooms, open shops, buy pepper, sell cloth. On Friday they find a quiet place and pray together. They make friends at the market.
Some marry and stay. A teacher among them starts answering questions from curious neighbors. Nobody marches in.
No banners. A new part of the path begins here: East and Southeast Asia. It begins with people who came to sell things.

teach.b: Today, the call to prayer sounds across Indonesia and Malaysia. And yet, in much of the region, the faith did not arrive with a conquering army. It came along the trade routes of the Indian Ocean.
Historians point to merchants from Arabia, Persia, India and China, and to Sufi teachers who traveled with them.

teach.h: PORT BY PORT, RULER BY RULER.
teach.b: It came slowly, port by port. Rulers of trading towns took up Islam, and their courts drew scholars.

The traveler Ibn Battuta describes stopping at a port in Sumatra called Samudra and meeting its Muslim sultan, a ruler who loved to sit with scholars and debate. Why would merchants make good messengers?
Partly because Islam has a lot to say about trade. Tradition remembers the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, as a merchant before his call.
The Qur'an tells believers not to consume one another's wealth wrongly, but to trade by mutual consent.
And of the Friday prayer it says, in Pickthall's translation: "And when the prayer is ended, then disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty." Prayer, then the market.
A saying of the Prophet in Sahih al-Bukhari says that when buyer and seller are truthful and make things clear, their deal is blessed, and when they hide and lie, the blessing is wiped out.
A merchant who weighs fairly, keeps his word, and closes the shop for prayer is a kind of sermon nobody has to preach.
As the story is often told, neighbors watched how these traders lived before they listened to what they believed.

how: Muslim teaching on trade stresses honest weights, clear terms and keeping one's word, and in Southeast Asia, as elsewhere, Muslim traders may close their shops for Friday prayer and reopen afterward.

soldiers who conquered the islands port by port

games.q: you're a Muslim merchant in a Sumatran port, waiting weeks for the wind. curious neighbors ask about your faith. what do you do?
o: argue with them in the market.
trade fairly, keep your word, and pray where they can see.
games.why: as the story is often told, neighbors watched how traders lived before they listened. truthful trade, in the hadith, is blessed.

practice: Think about the exchanges in your week: what you buy, sell, get paid for or promise, a job, a favor, a bill you split. Is there one where you've been a little less than clear?
Don't scold yourself; just name it, and picture what clear would look like, and if you pray, ask for honest hands.
